title: Stage 8 Science: The Tests and How to Prepare
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Science 0893 · Start here
summary: How Cambridge Lower Secondary science tests work — two 45-minute papers, question styles, mark-scheme words and results — and how to use this Stage 8 course to prepare.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: This course covers the whole Cambridge Lower Secondary Science Stage 8 curriculum (framework code 0893).
Thinking and Working Scientifically: models, planning, carrying out enquiries, analysing and evaluating (8TWSm, 8TWSp, 8TWSc, 8TWSa)
Biology: joints and muscles, blood, breathing, diet, respiration, ecosystems (8Bs, 8Bp, 8Be)
Chemistry: atoms, purity, concentration, chromatography, word equations, energy changes, reactivity, salts (8Cm, 8Cp, 8Cc)
Physics: speed, forces, moments, pressure, diffusion, light and colour, magnetism (8Pf, 8Ps, 8Pe)
Earth and space: Earth's magnetic field, resources, climate, galaxies and asteroids (8ESp, 8ESc, 8ESs)
Science in Context (8SIC) is taught through the lessons but Cambridge says it is not directly assessed.

blocks.text: Written by Mohamed Abdelkriem for students in British and international schools, and for their parents. Read this page first: it explains the tests you will meet, how they are marked, and how to use the rest of the course.
Which test, and when?

The **Cambridge Lower Secondary Checkpoint Science** test has the code **0893** (the same code as the curriculum framework) and two papers, **0893/01** and **0893/02**. It is set and marked by Cambridge. Very important for Stage 8 students: **the Checkpoint test is taken at the end of Stage 9**, and since May 2023 it assesses **Stage 9 only**. (The older tests with code 1113 belonged to the previous curriculum, so do not worry if you see old papers with that code.)

So why study Stage 8 in Checkpoint style? Because **Stage 9 builds on Stage 8**: you cannot understand Stage 9 respiration, atoms or forces without the Stage 8 ideas. And in Stage 8 your school is likely to give you **end-of-year tests in the same style** as Checkpoint. Cambridge makes **Lower Secondary Progression Tests** for Stages 7, 8 and 9. They are **marked by your teachers in school**, and schools can use them at any time in the year. This course prepares you for those Stage 8 tests and builds the base for Checkpoint at the end of Stage 9.

rows: 45 minutes each (both on the same day)
Paper 1 cover: "You may use a calculator."
Ask your teacher — bring one to practise with

blocks.text: Questions on **each** strand can appear on **both** papers: there is biology in Paper 1 and in Paper 2, and the same for chemistry, physics, and Earth and space. Thinking and Working Scientifically skills appear all through both papers — a question about blood may ask you to name a variable, read a graph or spot an anomalous result.

The front cover of a Checkpoint paper tells you to **answer all questions**, to write in the space provided, to use a **black or dark blue pen** (an HB pencil is allowed for diagrams and graphs), not to use correction fluid or an erasable pen, and to **show all your working**. The number of marks for each part is shown in square brackets, for example **[2]**.
How to use your 45 minutes

50 marks in 45 minutes gives you about **54 seconds per mark** (45 × 60 = 2700 seconds; 2700 ÷ 50 = 54). Use the marks as a clock: by about 18 minutes you should have answered roughly 20 marks' worth.

items: Read the **stem** (the information at the start of each question). Later parts often depend on it.
Look at the **marks**. [1] = one fact or one word. [2] = two separate points, or a point and a reason. [3] = three points, or a calculation with formula, working and unit.
Underline the **command word**: name, state, describe, explain, suggest, calculate, predict, compare.
Answer **every** part. A blank space can never score; a sensible answer often can.
If you are stuck, mark the question, move on, and come back at the end.
Keep the last 3–5 minutes to check units, the number of ticks, and that each [2] answer has two points.

rows: Give a short answer, no reason needed
Say what happens or what the data shows
"As the temperature increases, the time decreases."
Say what happens AND why (use because / so)
"The arm bends because the biceps contracts and pulls the forearm up."
Use your knowledge in a new situation; more than one answer may be right
"The thermometer may not have been read at eye level."
Work out a number; show working and give the unit
Say what you think will happen, using science
"The magnet will pick up more paperclips, because more coils make a stronger field."

blocks.text: Question styles you will meet
Real Cambridge Lower Secondary science papers use the styles below. Every lesson page in this course practises them.

rows: "Label parts A, B and C of the cell."
Use the exact science word; a line must point clearly to the part.
"Choose words from the list to complete the sentences."
Each word may be used once, more than once or not at all — read the instruction.
Tick exactly the number asked. An extra tick can cancel a correct one.
"Draw a line from each part of the blood to its job."
Use a ruler. One line from each box unless told otherwise.
"Complete the word equation for magnesium burning."
Reactants on the left, products on the right, an arrow (→) not an equals sign.
"Calculate the average speed. Show your working. Give the unit."
Write the formula, put the numbers in, then the answer and unit.
"Use the graph to find the solubility at 40 °C."
Draw construction lines on the graph and read the scale carefully.
"Plot the results on the grid and draw a line of best fit."
Plot each point as a small cross (×) exactly; use a sharp pencil.
"As … increases, … increases/decreases" + numbers from the data.
Give the fact AND the reason; one marking point for each idea.
"Suggest one improvement to Sara's method and explain why."
Name the change and say how it makes the results more accurate or reliable.

blocks.text: Understanding the mark scheme
Mark schemes have four columns: **Question, Answer, Marks, Further information**. These signs and words tell the examiner what to accept. Knowing them helps you write answers that get every mark.

rows: Separates different answers that each earn the same mark.
Answer A / answer B: either one is fine — do not write both if you are unsure.
Words or units in brackets do not have to be written.
"(red) blood cells": "blood cells" alone would do, but writing more is safer.
That exact word is needed for the mark.
Another answer the examiner will also give the mark for.
Different correct wordings are fine — the science must be right.
A wrong answer, or one that contradicts a correct one.
Writing a correct and a wrong answer together loses the mark.
Extra words that are not relevant: no mark, but no penalty.
Unrelated extras do not lose marks — but they waste time.
A mistake in an early part is not punished again in a later part.
Always finish later parts using your earlier answer, even if you are unsure of it.
The answer can be said the other way round.
"Copper is less reactive than zinc" = "zinc is more reactive than copper".

blocks.text: Three more helpful rules: a science word **spelled the way it sounds** is usually given the mark ("haemoglobbin" is clearly haemoglobin); **grammar is not marked**, only the science; and **marking points are independent** — you can get the second mark even if you miss the first. "**Show your working**" means write the formula and the numbers you used: if the final answer is wrong, the working can still earn marks.
Worked examples: how marks are given

**Worked example 1** — a 1-mark naming question
Question: Name the part of the blood that carries oxygen. [1]

rows: "(blood)" would be in brackets in the mark scheme — not needed.
red blood cells and white blood cells
White blood cells do not carry oxygen: the wrong extra contradicts the right answer.
Too vague: the question asks for the part of the blood.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 2** — a 2-mark explanation
Question: Explain why the knee needs two muscles to bend and straighten the leg. [2]

items: Count the marks: [2] means two separate points.
Point 1: muscles can only **pull** (contract); they cannot push.
Point 2: so one muscle pulls to bend the leg and the other pulls to straighten it — they are an **antagonistic pair**.
Full answer: "Muscles can only pull, not push, so one muscle (the hamstring) contracts to bend the knee and the other (the quadriceps) contracts to straighten it."

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** "One muscle pushes and one pulls." This is wrong science and scores 0.

**Worked example 3** — a calculation and error carried forward
Question: A cyclist travels 600 m in 120 s. (a) Calculate the speed. Give the unit. [2] (b) How far does she travel in 300 s at the same speed? [1]

items: (a) speed = distance ÷ time = 600 ÷ 120 = **5 m/s**. One mark for the working or the number, one mark for the unit.
(b) distance = speed × time = 5 × 300 = **1500 m**.

Suppose a student wrote 600 ÷ 120 = 6 m/s in (a) — the number is wrong. In (b) they write 6 × 300 = 1800 m. They used their own (a) answer correctly, so with **ecf** they still get the mark in (b). Never leave (b) blank because you doubt (a).

blocks.text:
**Worked example 4** — or reverse argument (ora)
Question: Zinc reacts with dilute acid but copper does not. What does this tell you about the reactivity of zinc and copper? [1]

items: "Zinc is more reactive than copper." — 1 mark.
"Copper is less reactive than zinc." — also 1 mark (ora: the same idea said the other way round).
"Zinc is reactive." — 0 marks: there is no comparison.

blocks.title: For parents
blocks.text: Look at the strand results, not only the total. A student with "High" in Biology but "Aspiring" in Physics knows exactly where to work. Each section of this course matches one strand, so you can choose the pages for the weaker strand and use the practice quizzes on them.
Thinking and Working Scientifically (TWS)

TWS is the skills strand. It is reported as a strand of its own, and it is mixed into almost every question. At Stage 8 it has four parts. The page **Thinking and Working Scientifically** teaches all of them in detail; here is the big picture with one example of each.

rows: Explain what an analogy is and use one; use symbols and formulae.
"The heart is like a pump." Writing speed = distance ÷ time, or H_{2}O for water.
Decide if a hypothesis is testable, predict using science, plan investigations, write risk assessments.
"More coils will make the electromagnet stronger, because…" Not every investigation can be a fair test.
Classify and use keys, choose equipment, measure accurately, repeat readings, judge secondary sources for bias, record results.
Reading a measuring cylinder at eye level; noticing that an advert from a company may be biased.
Describe trends, find anomalous results, say if predictions were accurate, make conclusions with limitations, suggest improvements, present data.
"As the coils increase from 10 to 60, the paperclips increase from 3 to 18. The result at 40 coils is anomalous."

blocks.title: أهم حاجة في الامتحان
blocks.text: اختبار Checkpoint في العلوم بيتعمل في آخر Stage 9، لكن امتحانات آخر السنة في Stage 8 بتيجي بنفس الشكل: ورقتين، كل ورقة ٤٥ دقيقة و٥٠ درجة. بص على الدرجة بين القوسين [ ]: لو [2] يبقى لازم تكتب نقطتين (معلومة + سبب). ومتكتبش إجابتين واحدة صح وواحدة غلط — هتاخد صفر.
How to use this course

The course follows the curriculum strand by strand. Each lesson page teaches one or two objectives with diagrams, key words in Arabic, worked examples, common mistakes, exam tips and an interactive quiz with full solutions.

rows: This page; Thinking and Working Scientifically
Week 1 (and come back to TWS often)
Joints and muscles; blood; breathing and gas exchange; diet; respiration; ecosystems
Atoms; purity, concentration and chromatography; word equations and energy; reactivity; products and solubility
Speed and graphs; forces and moments; pressure and diffusion; reflection and refraction; colour; magnetism
Magnetic field and resources; climate; galaxies and asteroids
Three full tests: Paper 1 and Paper 2, 45 minutes and 50 marks each
The last weeks before your end-of-year test

items: Read the **In the curriculum** box so you know exactly what you must be able to do.
Learn the **key words** (English + Arabic). Science marks are lost on vocabulary more than anything else.
Cover the answer to each **worked example**, try it yourself, then compare line by line.
Read **Common mistakes** and **How Checkpoint asks this** before the quiz.
Do the **Practice** quiz with no notes. Read every solution, even for questions you got right.
One week later, do the quiz again. Write the topics you got wrong in a notebook and revise them before the practice tests.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Writing one point for a [2] question. Two marks need two separate ideas.
Giving a number without a unit, or with the wrong unit (m/s for speed, N for force).
Writing two answers "to be safe" — a wrong one cancels the right one.
Describing data with no numbers. Quote values from the table or graph.
Using everyday words ("the muscle gets small") instead of science words ("the muscle contracts").
Leaving a later part blank because an earlier part was hard — ecf can still give you the mark.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: Most questions start with a short story: a student doing an investigation, a table of results or a diagram. Read it twice.
Almost every question mixes a topic with a TWS skill: variables, predictions, trends, anomalies, improvements.
Calculations: write the formula first, then substitute, then the answer with its unit.
Graphs: label both axes with units, use more than half the grid, plot crosses exactly, draw a smooth line or curve of best fit.
"Explain" questions: one marking point per idea — use "because" and "so".

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: The Stage 8 Science tests: quick quiz
blocks.intro: 8 questions on the tests, the mark scheme and TWS. Full solutions are shown after you check.

questions.q: When do students take the Cambridge Lower Secondary Checkpoint Science test (0893)?
questions.e: Since May 2023 the Checkpoint tests assess the final stage of Lower Secondary only — Stage 9. Stage 8 students usually sit end-of-year tests in the same style.

questions.q: How many minutes long is each science paper (Checkpoint Paper 1 and Paper 2, and the Stage 8 Progression Test papers)?
Each paper is worth 50 marks. How many marks are there in total for the two papers?
A paper has 50 marks and lasts 45 minutes. About how many seconds do you have for each mark? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
questions.e: 45 minutes = 45 × 60 = 2700 seconds. 2700 ÷ 50 = 54 seconds per mark. So a [2] part should take about 2 minutes at most.

questions.q: In a mark scheme, the answer is written as: "oxygen / O_{2}". What does the / mean?
c: The second answer gets half a mark
questions.e: The slash separates alternative answers for the same marking point: "oxygen" or "O_{2}" each earns the mark.

questions.q: In a science mark scheme, what do the letters "ecf" stand for?
questions.e: ecf = error carried forward: if your part (a) answer is wrong but you use it correctly in part (b), you can still get the mark in (b).

questions.q: The question asks for one gas that plants take in for photosynthesis. Ali writes "carbon dioxide or oxygen". How many marks does he get out of 1?
c: 0, because a wrong answer contradicts the right one
1, because both gases are in the air
questions.e: A correct answer with a wrong one beside it is a contradiction ("do not accept"), so it scores 0. Write only the answer you are sure of.

questions.p:
Question 8
Youssef investigates how the temperature of water affects the time a sugar cube takes to dissolve.
questions.q: Which is the independent variable (the one he changes)?
c: the mass of the sugar cube
questions.e: He chooses and changes the temperature, so it is the independent variable. The time is the dependent variable (measured). Mass of sugar and volume of water are control variables.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Checkpoint Science (0893) is taken at the end of Stage 9; Stage 8 end-of-year tests use the same style.
Two papers, 45 minutes and 50 marks each; all strands and TWS can appear on both.
About 54 seconds per mark: let the [marks] tell you how much to write.
Mark-scheme language: / = alternatives, ( ) = not needed, underlined = exact word, ecf, ora.
Show working and units; never write a right and a wrong answer together.
